subject: the 8 sentences check_translation_agreement.py still flags across the shipped corpus

method.shape: three independent lenses per sentence (Japanese correctness, learner harm, translation fidelity), then an adversary whose default is to refuse the change — the review shape that has held for six content batches
method.lensVotes: 24 votes: 9 false-positive, 15 harmless-variation, 0 real-defect. The adversary overruled nobody; it agreed with a unanimous panel.
method.negativeControl: REQUIRED, and run. A panel that returns 'nothing to fix' is indistinguishable from a broken panel until it is shown to fire. The same three lenses were given four deliberately-corrupted pairs (a verb flipped bought->sold, a stated number 三人 rendered as 五个, an explicit 私は一人で rendered as 'we all together', a dropped negation) plus one clean shipped pair. Result: 12/12 corrupted votes returned real-defect AND named the correct defective side; 3/3 clean votes returned harmless-variation. The panel discriminates.

whyNoneWereChanged: In all eight, the Japanese has a ZERO SUBJECT. Neither translation contradicts the source, because the source does not state what they differ about — both are fillings of a slot Japanese leaves empty, and back-translating either produces correct Japanese for the same scene.

Three of the eight are not disagreements at all: the checker's first-person regex includes the possessive \bmy\b, so 'The family celebrated my grandfather's 60th birthday' trips a rule about SUBJECTS while its subject is 'the family'. (n1-b664, n1-b1814, n5-g083.)

The app shows ONE translation at a time — VocabEntry.exampleTranslation(for:) returns the zh string or the en string, never both — so a learner has to switch interface language and re-draw the same card to see any difference at all. The contradiction the checker describes is not visible to the reader it was meant to protect.
The typing target carries no pronoun in any of the eight, so no learner ever practises the disputed word.
Correcting a shipped translation is an overwrite of reviewed content: it costs a manifest and a re-review. Nicer wording is not the bar.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says I, zh says 我们
flags.note: Both sides say 'we'. The regex fired on the possessive in 'my deceased grandfather'; bare 祖父 is the humble in-group form, so the possessor is licensed on both sides.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says I, zh says 我们
flags.note: Subject is 'The family' / 我们一家人 — the same referent. Fired on 'my grandfather'.

flags.headword: 顕微鏡 / けんびきょう
flags.objection: subject differs: en says I, zh says 我们
flags.note: A genuine surface difference, not an artifact — but the JP states no subject at all, and a classroom scene reads naturally either per-student or collectively.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says we, zh says 我
flags.note: 仲間と一緒に fixes the COMPOSITION of the acting party, not its number. The English 'We … together with friends' is mildly redundant; wording, not meaning.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says I, zh says 我们
flags.note: The subject of います is 双子 on all three sides; the person marker is only the possessor of the class. 我们班 is the obligatory Chinese rendering of 私のクラス — 我的班 is unnatural.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says we, zh says 我
flags.note: Zero subject in the JP; plain-past 要求した encodes neither person nor number. This one was also used as the CLEAN control in the negative-control run, and all three lenses independently returned harmless there too.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says I, zh says 我们
flags.note: Two clauses. The English 'I'm' belongs to the tired clause, the Chinese 我们 to the ましょう clause; both renderings are correct.

flags.objection: subject differs: en says I, zh says 我们
flags.note: The Chinese reframes 私は三人兄弟です as 我们家有三兄弟姐妹 — a recast, and the widest gap of the eight. Still not a contradiction: the family described is the same one, and the count is preserved.

checkerNote: The \bmy\b clause in check_translation_agreement.py's en_i regex causes 3 of its 8 flags. It was NOT removed. That file already documents seven failed refinements and one deletion; a change calibrated on eight sentences and shipped against 6,737 is how the number half of this checker died. If it is ever revisited, calibrate on the full corpus first.
